# Exact affine-radius reduction for half-integer simplex chains in every dimension

This is a proved reduction for the deficit of ONE fixed original
halfspace. It does not assert that every affine-radius deficit is
nonnegative and does not prove arbitrary mixed-integer OC.

## Theorem

Let d>=1, m>=0, R>0, and let

    T_d = conv(0,e_1,...,e_d),       V_d=|T_d|=1/d!,
    Gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d,            t=R/(d+1).

Suppose r_0=R>=r_1>=...>=r_m>=0 and the successive radius drops are
nondecreasing. At integer bases -h and h+1, h=0,...,m, take the fibers
r_h T_d. Fix a vector u with u_i>=0 and sum_i u_i=1, and beta>=0.
The point

    y=(0,t,...,t)

is the centroid of the actual fiber at base zero. Consider its fixed
closed halfspace

    -beta z+u.x>=t.

For s in R and r>=0 define the exact normalized cap volume

    F_r(s)=|rT_d intersect {u.x>=s}|/V_d,

and define

    G_h(r)=F_r(t-beta h)+F_r(t+beta(h+1))-Gamma_d r^d.

If m>=1, there is a slope a in [0,R/m] such that, with ell_h=R-a h,

    G_h(ell_h)<=G_h(r_h)       for every h=0,...,m.       (1)

The center, integer bases, continuous normal, tilt beta, central radius,
and number of fiber pairs remain fixed. The replacement radii define
another convex-compatible source. When m=0 there is nothing to replace.

Since the exact total mass is 2V_d sum_h r_h^d, the original cap's
deficit from the desired Gamma_d/2 fraction is V_d sum_h G_h(r_h).
Consequently any negative original deficit gives a negative affine-radius
deficit for this very same halfspace. No preservation of total mass is
asserted or needed for this implication.

## 1. Radial derivative and unique deficit minimizer

Let Theta be uniform on the opposite facet

    Delta={theta_i>=0:sum_i theta_i=1}

and set U=u.Theta. For d=1 this simply means Theta=1 and U=1.
For every d, U>=0, U<=max_i u_i, and E U=1/d. Write

    T(v)=P(U>=v).

Radial integration from the vertex zero gives, for s>0,

    F_r(s)=d integral_0^r w^(d-1) T(s/w) dw.             (2)

Indeed a uniform point in rT_d can be written w Theta, with normalized
radial volume density d w^(d-1)dw. This formula can equally be obtained
by the affine Jacobian in facet barycentric coordinates. It uses the
uniform (d-1)-dimensional facet measure, which is independent of w.
For s<=0, F_r(s)=r^d. The value at r=0 is zero in both formulas.

Fix a real h>=0 and put

    q=t-beta h,              p=t+beta(h+1)>=q.

If q<=0, then

    G_h(r)=(1-Gamma_d)r^d+F_r(p)

is strictly increasing for r>=0, and its unique minimizer is rho_h=0.

Suppose q>0. First assume that u is not constant on Delta, necessarily
d>=2. The distribution of U is atomless, its support is
[min_i u_i,max_i u_i], and its tail is strictly decreasing between
these endpoints. Atomlessness follows because each level is a proper
affine hyperplane in Delta. Strict decrease follows because the inverse
image of each nonempty open subinterval of the projection contains a
nonempty relatively open subset of the facet. Thus (2) is continuously
differentiable for r>0 and

    G_h'(r)=d r^(d-1) [T(q/r)+T(p/r)-Gamma_d].           (3)

The bracket is continuous and nondecreasing, equals -Gamma_d for all
sufficiently small r, and tends to 2-Gamma_d>0 as r tends to infinity.
At any zero, the first tail lies in [Gamma_d/2,Gamma_d], hence strictly
between zero and one. Its threshold is therefore in the interior of
the support. Increasing r strictly increases that first tail until it
reaches one, and decreasing r strictly decreases it until it reaches
zero. It follows that the zero is unique; denote it by rho_h>0.
The bracket is strictly negative below rho_h and strictly positive
above it. Hence G_h is strictly decreasing on [0,rho_h] and strictly
increasing on [rho_h,infinity).

If u is constant, its normalization gives u_i=1/d and U=1/d. Directly
from (2), for s>0,

    F_r(s)=(r^d-(ds)^d)_+.

Since p>=q>0 and 0<Gamma_d<1, the first derivative on every interval
between the knots is negative before r=dq and positive afterwards.
The function is continuous at the knots. Thus the same strict
unimodality holds, with the exact minimizer

    rho_h=dq.

This includes d=1. In all cases, there is a uniquely defined minimizer
rho_h, with no differentiability assumption on h -> rho_h.

## 2. A uniform strict intercept bound

For the nonconstant case, apply the ordinary Grünbaum inequality in
dimension d-1 to the facet Delta at its centroid. Its projected mean
is 1/d, and therefore

    T(1/d)>=Gamma_(d-1)>Gamma_d.                         (4)

Here Gamma_k=(k/(k+1))^k for k>=1; the strict inequality for adjacent
positive dimensions follows from strict decrease of
x -> (x/(x+1))^x on x>0. For d=2 the facet bound is the usual interval
centroid half-mass inequality. The constant case has already been
handled directly and requires no dimension-zero invocation.

At the minimizer, T(q/rho_h)<=Gamma_d. Comparing with (4) gives

    q/rho_h>1/d,       rho_h<d q             (q>0,
                                                      u nonconstant).

For a constant u equality rho_h=dq holds. Consequently, universally,

    0<=rho_h<=d(t-beta h)_+,
    rho_0<=dR/(d+1)<R.                                 (5)

In particular, whenever q>0,

    q/rho_h>=1/d>t/R=1/(d+1),       rho_h<R.             (6)

Only the strict comparison with t/R is needed below. No root derivative,
B-spline density formula, regularity of a quantile, or smoothness of u
is used.

## 3. The minimizing-radius secants are strictly ordered

Define for real h>0

    b(h)=(R-rho_h)/h.

Then b(h)>0 and b is strictly decreasing. The constant-u case follows
directly from (5): on q>0 it equals
(R-dt)/h+d beta, and on q<=0 it equals R/h, with matching values at
the transition. We give the nonconstant case without an implicit
function argument.

Fix 0<h_1<h_2. If rho_(h_1)=0, then q(h_1)<=0, so rho_(h_2)=0 and
b(h_2)=R/h_2<R/h_1=b(h_1). Assume rho_(h_1)>0 and set

    a=b(h_1),        ell(x)=R-a x.

At x=h_1, ell=rho_(h_1). The strict threshold comparison (6) gives

    (t-beta h_1)/(R-a h_1)>t/R,
    a t>beta R.                                         (7)

For x with ell(x)>0, direct differentiation of two ordinary rational
functions gives

    d/dx [(t-beta x)/ell(x)] = (a t-beta R)/ell(x)^2 >0,
    d/dx [(t+beta(x+1))/ell(x)]
                      = [beta R+a(t+beta)]/ell(x)^2 >0.  (8)

If ell(h_2)>0, then (7) also implies q(h_2)>0: the line reaches zero
strictly before t-beta x can reach zero when beta>0, and the assertion
is immediate when beta=0. Both thresholds in (8) have increased from
their minimizing values at h_1. The first tail strictly decreases,
because it starts strictly between zero and one. The second tail does
not increase. Hence

    T(q(h_2)/ell(h_2))+T(p(h_2)/ell(h_2))<Gamma_d.

By the unique root characterization in Section 1,
ell(h_2)<rho_(h_2), giving b(h_2)<a=b(h_1).

If ell(h_2)<0, the same strict conclusion follows simply from
rho_(h_2)>=0>ell(h_2). If ell(h_2)=0, (7) gives q(h_2)>0, whence
rho_(h_2)>0=ell(h_2), again giving strictness. This proves the stated
monotonicity across all branch changes, support knots, zero-radius
transitions, and beta=0.

## 4. The affine replacement

For h=1,...,m put

    a_h=(R-r_h)/h,       b_h=(R-rho_h)/h.

The a_h are nonnegative and nondecreasing: they average the first h
successive nonnegative drops of a concave radius sequence. The b_h
are positive and strictly decreasing by Section 3. Therefore the set
of indices where a_h<=b_h is an initial segment 1,...,k, possibly empty
or the whole set. Equivalently r_h>=rho_h on that segment and
r_h<=rho_h afterwards.

If k=m choose a=a_m. For every h, a_h<=a<=b_m<=b_h, so
rho_h<=ell_h<=r_h. If k=0 choose a=b_1. For every h,
b_h<=a<=a_1<=a_h, so r_h<=ell_h<=rho_h.

If 0<k<m choose any number in the nonempty interval

    max(a_k,b_(k+1)) <= a <= min(b_k,a_(k+1)).            (9)

Nonemptiness follows from the two monotonicities and the defining
inequalities at k and k+1. For h<=k, (9) gives
rho_h<=ell_h<=r_h. For h>=k+1, it gives
r_h<=ell_h<=rho_h. In every case the strict unimodality established
in Section 1 yields G_h(ell_h)<=G_h(r_h). At h=0 the radius remains
R, so equality holds. This proves (1).

The selected a is nonnegative. Each ell_h is between two nonnegative
radii, so ell_m>=0 and a<=R/m. On the full base interval [-m,m+1],
the piecewise affine interpolation of these paired radii is nonnegative
and concave, with a flat central pair. The set

    { (z,x): -m<=z<=m+1, x_i>=0, sum_i x_i<=ell(z) }

is a compact convex body with exactly the replacement simplex fibers
at integer bases. It has nonempty interior because R>0 on the central
interval. This proves convex compatibility, membership of the original
center, and the exact mass interpretation claimed in the theorem.

## 5. Scope and remaining task

This gives a dimension-independent geometric mechanism for the exact
affine-radius reduction previously obtained by explicit quadratic
formulas in dimension two. It includes repeated normal coordinates,
zero normal coordinates, constant facet projections, zero outer radii,
all beta>=0, and support endpoints. All halfspaces considered are the
original closed oblique halfspaces with their shared tilt. Their
fiber cap boundaries have zero d-volume; the only facet projection
atom is the constant case treated directly.

The reduction leaves a concrete affine-radius cap inequality to prove.
It does not by itself establish that inequality or extend these simplex
chains to arbitrary convex fibers.
